newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish central bank to cut bond issuance in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Danish central bank to cut bond issuance in 1997.

text.p: Denmark's central bank on Tuesday announced a sharp drop in the government's estimated gross domestic financing needs to about 69.9 billion crowns ($11.8 billion) in 1997 from 98.3 billion in 1996.
Earlier on Tuesday, Denmark's Finance Ministry cut its estimates for the 1996 and 1997 state budget deficits to 25 billion crowns and 5.9 billion crowns respectively.
The ministry's new forecasts follow an encouraging Economy Ministry forecast earlier in December which gave Denmark's economy a clean bill of health.

Analysts expected actual government bond issuance of around 82 billion crowns in 1997 compared with 105.5 billion in 1996 and said that the reduction in paper was likely to push yields down, which in turn would probably make shares more attractive and boost their prices.
The small Danish stock market, where the major banks' shares play a prominent role, is heavily influenced by bond movements.

"Especially at the start of the new year there will be a marked rise in demand for government bonds because the National Bank will not issue so many," Banque Indosuez economist Kai Lindberg told the Danish daily Berlingske Tidende.

"We do not think there are enough alternatives to absorb capital so there are real grounds for a fall in yields. Mortgage bonds can take up some of the surplus money and the stock market will benefit from some investors moving into shares," he added.
Nykredit Bank's John Madsen saw Danish bonds outperforming German Bunds and expected the Danish 10-year bond, yielding 6.69 percent on Tuesday, to yield 6.50 percent by March 1997.

"We think that the reduced financing requirement, together with a generally positive market in the first half of 1997 will push Danish yields a bit further down. Only in the second half will economic condition here and elsewhere in Europe send them up again," Madsen told Berlingske.
The central bank on Tuesday said it would open a new four percent bond series, maturing on February 15, 2000, on January 7 1997 and a five percent bond due August 15, 2005 would open on January 14.
The sale of bonds would begin at 1000 GMT on each date through the Copenhagen Stock Exchange match system, it added.

The sale of six percent 1999 treasury notes would continue during the first six months of 1997 and there would be regular issues of short-term paper, it said, but the existing fixed programme of issuing a new note every six months would cease.
The bank said that ordinary repayments on outstanding government bonds and treasury notes would be lower in 1997 than in 1998 and it would therefore aim at spreading its refinancing.

The statement said that sales of the six percent 2002, the seven percent 2007 and seven percent 2024 bonds would continue unaltered. There would also be monthly auctions and a new 9-month treasury bill every three months.
A new nine-month bill would open on December 20, 1996, it added and access would continue to be given to location swaps for a nominal two billion crowns in each of the new series.

The bank said that ordinary payments on outstanding government bonds and treasury notes would be lower in 1997 than in 1998 and it would therefore aim to spread refinancing by making repurchases in the series maturing in 1998, if market conditions allowed.
As in previous years, securities maturing in 1997 could be repurchased in that year, it added.
